Each round consists of twelve tricks played, and at the end of each round, a score is awarded based on the number of tricks and cards acquired. Once one player (or team) reaches 30 points, the game ends, and the side with the most points wins! Number of players: 2,4 Game duration: 38 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Lunar and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Round End 4 Game End 5 2 Player Variant Overview A twist on the traditional Trick Taking game, where one partner plays the Suit and the other plays the Rank, attempting to combine their cards into winning combinations Deck Composition The deck is composed of 48 cards: 3 of each rank card (without suits) in ranks 1-8 6 of each suit card (without ranks) in 4 suits (wolf, owl, lynx & bat) Turn To start off, each player picks 2 Rank cards and 2 Suit cards from their starting hand to exchange with their partner Secondly, beginning with the start player, players flip one trump card facedown until only one remains faceup and this becomes the Trump suit Then Tricks commence The starting player can play any card they desire The first player of a team can also play either a Suit card or Rank card, whilst the second player on the same team has to play the other i.e. if teammate 1 plays a Suit then teammate 2 must play a Rank The first player to play a Suit determines the lead Suit of the trick, note that this does NOT have to be the start player nor the start team e.g. team A Player 1 plays Rank, team B Player 1 plays Suit, team B has determined Suit Once Lead Suit is determined, the next player to play Suit must play the same Suit if they have it, or any if they do not hold a copy of Lead Suit After a Trick is completed, determine the winner of the trick as follows: If the teams played the same suit, the highest rank wins, if tied the team who played last wins If the teams played different suits, and one was the trump suit, the team with the trump suit wins If the team played different suits, with no trump played, the team who determined the Lead Suit (i.e. played Suit earliest) wins The team who wins advances their team marker one space and retains any cards played by any team which contain the star icon The leader of the winning team starts the next trick Round End The round ends when players run out of hand cards Each team scores points based on the stars next to their position on the team track In addition, each team scores a point for each retained star card A new round begins Game End The game ends if, at round end, at least one team has scored at least 30 points The team with the most points, wins! If tied, continue playing rounds until there is a clear winner 2 Player Variant There is a neutral Sky area with its own 'hand' of cards In each round, each player has two turns, one where they must play Suit or Rank, and the other where they play what they did not play before In addition, one card must come from their hidden hand and the other must come from the shared Sky 'hand', again the order is player choice but the second turn must be played from where they did not play before In regards to following Suit, ONLY consider the cards in the area you plan to (or must) play from e.g. if there is a lead suit card in the Sky but none in your hand, you can choose to play a non-lead Suit from your hand. community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] I guess it's the polar opposite of Yokai Septet: a team game where there's no tension or excitement. And it borrows that awful scoring chart from Fox and the Forest. The 2p version was even worse, with how confusing it was, and I really dislike those public card markets everyone can play from.

[Rating: 3/10] Decent game where, as a team, one has to play the suit and the other plays the rank, and then the two teams compare which combo is stronger.

[Rating: 3/10] Sometimes you can have a neat idea, but it doesn't turn in to an interesting game.   That's Lunar's mistake. They thought by making each person on a team play the suit and number of a card separately for tricks, you'd have a cool game. Unfortunately due to the turn order and other rules regarding the tricks, you're too often left without particularly interesting decisions.

[Rating: 4/10] Kickstarted  Promos/Expansions: - Lunar: 2023 Promo Upgrade  I've only played this one using the two player variant and its terrible. I couldn't tell you if I was just missing the strategic choices or if there were truly none to make. I'll hold off final judgement until I play with 4.

[Rating: 4/10] Tried at 2 and at 4 and it just fell kinda flat at both player counts. Often times you just don't have any choices (which is already a consideration in trick taking games) but the lack of choices seems even more severe because of how the values and suits are split up. I like all of the ideas presented in this game, but it feels like the actual game created from them just isn't very fun.

[Rating: 4/10] This was not a good 2 player game.  It's too easy to trap someone in a loop.  Not scoring yet because the concept is interesting and I think it could be good at 4  I will say that the deluxe metal components are pretty sweet and completely unnecessary.  Just heavy chonky metal but I really liked it  Edit: it seemed to have a similar problem at 4, which is that you can just get trapped in a cycle. The lead player remaining the same on the team can really mess things up for the entire round. Not a fan of how it played out. But still gorgeous components and a cool theme/idea. The unfortunate part

[Rating: 4/10] A neat team based twist on trick taking. One player plays the number and one plays the suit. Unfortunately I think this just makes for a worse experience, in a genre I already don't love. Mostly because of how awkward it is to communicate anything. Plus it adds to that trick taking staple of turns with no choices. I can see how a group that developed their own saucy ways to share info could have a blast with it though.   The art direction is cool. It's like those cheesy retro animal t-shirts that we all know and love. The cover is much better than the card art unfortunately.

[Rating: 5/10] Partnership game, where you and your partner essentially play a single card to a round of tricks.  Teammate 1 can play either suit or number, and Teammate 2 plays the other.  It's a nice idea but it really feels constraining. The Allplay production is really nice, though.

[Rating: 5/10] Tragically, I think trick-taking games are just not for me. This one, while exceptionally pretty, was a struggle for my ADHD brain to keep track of. Beautiful game, decent at 2 player, and ultimately not healthy for my relationship.

[Rating: 5/10] A trick taking game where players play as teams and on your turn you're either playing a suit or the numbered card to determine a winner of the trick. Players have control of the trump suit but scoring is based on number of tricks won and cross referenced with a static table.
